clue.text: Ridicule dummy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to make fun of someone
second meaning: imitation or sham, as in a practice run

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like an insult hurled at someone, but each is a separate meaning of one short word, a verb and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as a verb for making fun of someone and as an adjective for something imitation, like a practice exam.

clue.text: Threaten nurse in club

indicators.note: something placed in another thing ends up surrounded by it

parts.note: a mace is a heavy club used as a weapon
EN is an Enrolled Nurse, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: Someone waves a club at a nurse to intimidate her.
explanation.walkthrough: Club suggests a golf or social club, but here it is a weapon, split open to take the nurse inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To menace someone is to intimidate them with a hint of harm, the same verb sense as to threaten.

clue.text: 13 making love before showing brains

indicators.note: to make one thing into another is to turn it into something else, so one letter is converted to others

parts.note: the answer to 13 across
love is nil in tennis, which looks like O
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Something about love showing up in the brain, as a neuroscientist might say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making' here means converting: the round letter for love in the 13 answer is made into the old word for before.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerebra is the plural of cerebrum, the main mass of the brain, so it stands for brains in the plural.

clue.text: Brute, maybe a strongman to some extent

indicators.note: only partly present, so just a portion of the running text is used

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A description of a hulking strongman as something of a brute.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through maybE A STrongman.
explanation.definitionFit: A brute is a savage person or animal, which is exactly what calling someone a beast conveys; the two are close synonyms.

clue.text: Faded out the answer to what started Norton on the radio

indicators.note: radio carries only sound, so the words are judged by how they are heard, not spelt

parts.words: the answer to what started Norton
parts.note: asked what started the name Norton, you would answer that N did

explanation.surface: A radio show presented by Graham Norton faded out at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Norton suggests the broadcaster Graham Norton, but the question is about the name's spelling: its first letter N did the starting, and 'N did' spoken aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that faded out came to a finish, so the past tense matches: both mean finished or stopped.

clue.text: Help stops every now and then

indicators.note: doing something every now and then means only at intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Help arrives only occasionally, stopping from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Help' reads as the subject of a sentence, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: SOS is the international distress signal, a call for help, so it stands for the cry itself.

clue.text: Thrill from essentially smacking naked skin first

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is its core, so the central letters are taken

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters stripped

indicators.note: stripped bare, with the outer covering removed, leaving the inside

parts.note: the two central letters of an eight-letter word

explanation.surface: A thrill from being smacked on the bare skin, a racy picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' says the letters from the skin go before those from the smacking, reversing the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: A kick is slang for a burst of excitement or pleasure, as in doing something for kicks.

clue.text: Clever clogs offloading with a barrow, once

indicators.note: to offload is to unload or get rid of, so letters are dropped

parts.note: a know-all is a clever clogs, British slang for a smart alec
W is the standard abbreviation for with
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smart alec unloads a wheelbarrow of old.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove W and A from KNOWALL to leave KNO-LL. Barrow looks like a wheelbarrow, but here it is the landform.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrow once meant a hill or mound in Old English, and a small rounded hill is still called by this word.

clue.text: More sterile, detailed Cleo — and Liz? Her husband's gone

indicators.note: read as de-tailed: with the tail cut off, so each word loses its last letter
the husband leaves, so the abbreviation for husband is removed

parts.note: the name without its last letter
the word without its last letter
the name without its last letter
the word without H, the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Elizabeth Taylor, who played Cleopatra, famously went through husbands; here one has just left.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Taylor played Cleo(patra) and married many times, which is the joke; 'detailed' clips the tail of Cleo, and and Liz, and Her loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile means free of germs, and the comparative of cleanly is a fair equivalent for more free of dirt.

clue.text: Pleasure ground from revolutionary Sudan, axed

indicators.note: taken from within the words, so the letters are lifted out of the running text
a revolution turns something round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: the letters run backwards through the end of the country's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A revolutionary regime in Sudan scraps a pleasure park.
explanation.walkthrough: Read sUDAN AXed backwards. Xanadu is Kubla Khan's summer palace in Coleridge's poem, where he 'did a stately pleasure-dome decree'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's poem made the place a byword for an idyllic, luxurious retreat, a literal pleasure garden of the Khan.

clue.text: Choice of sides from newsroom accepted as standard

indicators.note: offering a choice between two things puts the word for alternatives between them
the sides of a word are its two ends, so the outer letters are used

parts.note: the first and last letters
or is the word that offers a choice
A is an abbreviation for accepted

explanation.surface: A newsroom chooses which side of a story to take, according to its house standard.
explanation.walkthrough: A choice of the two sides of newsroom is 'N or M', which gives the first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A norma is a pattern or rule, the Latin root of norm, and also a carpenter's square used to check a standard angle.

clue.text: Kiss of death from Bambi, maybe defining animated story

indicators.note: to define is to mark out the limits of something, so one piece forms a boundary round the other

parts.note: Bambi is a famous fawn, an example of the animal

indicators.note: animated means brought to life and set moving, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: The death of Bambi's mother in the animated Disney film is the story's kiss of death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'animated story' looks like a description of the Disney film, but animated is the anagram signal and story is its fodder, placed inside DEER.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiss of death is whatever ruins something, so a destroyer, that which wrecks or brings about ruin, fits as a noun.

clue.text: It's commonly reputed, 22's guts churned over vacuous apology

indicators.note: churning stirs something up violently, so the letters are mixed
the guts of something are its insides, so only the inner letters are kept

parts.note: 22 across is SHYSTER; its insides without the first and last letters

indicators.note: empty of contents, so only the outer shell of letters remains

parts.note: only the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a crooked lawyer felt sick after a hollow apology.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the churned letters sit on top of AY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the standard way of passing on hearsay, attributing a claim to unnamed people, which is what commonly reputed means.

clue.text: Born in the jungle, ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the final letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the final letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Someone who was born in the jungle, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is used before a married woman's maiden name, as in Mrs Smith née Jones.
explanation.definitionFit: Née is French for born, and in English it introduces the family name a woman was born with.

clue.text: Government committee's firm support

parts.note: Co is short for company, a firm
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: A government committee is said to give firm backing to a policy.
explanation.walkthrough: COBRA (Cabinet Office Briefing Room A) is the British government's emergency committee, named after the room where it meets.
explanation.definitionFit: The UK crisis response group takes its name from the Whitehall briefing room it convenes in, making it a committee name.

clue.text: Genetic code — with two lines describing the old from the east Lancashire town

indicators.note: in an across clue, reading from the east means from right to left, backwards

parts.note: DNA carries the genetic code

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for line, twice
ye is an old spelling of the

explanation.surface: A genetics note about a family line from the east of a Lancashire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything is assembled first in clue order, the lines wrapped round the old word, then the whole string is read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Leyland is a town in Lancashire, a county in northwest England, known for building lorries and buses.

clue.text: Pursue mate — not in Kent area

indicators.note: 'not in' tells you those two letters are left out

parts.note: Cockney rhyming slang: china plate means mate
Kent is a county in the South East of England

explanation.surface: Someone is told to chase their friend who isn't in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang for mate (china plate = mate); drop IN to leave CHA, then add SE, the South East region where Kent lies.
explanation.definitionFit: To chase is to run after someone to catch them, the same verb sense as pursue.

clue.text: Awkwardly move a ball into empty goalmouth

indicators.note: putting something into another thing places it inside
an emptied word keeps only its shell, the first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters
a lump is a rounded mass, like a ball of dough
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clumsy footballer shuffles the ball into an unguarded goal.
explanation.walkthrough: The ball here is not a football but a rounded lump.
explanation.definitionFit: To galumph is to move in a clumsy, heavy, lumbering way, a word coined by Lewis Carroll.

clue.text: Start to giggle about head teacher

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter
as in arguing over, or about, something
a ness is a headland, a point of land jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: Pupils begin to giggle about the head teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head teacher' looks like a single phrase, but head is wordplay and teacher alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A governess is a woman employed to teach children in a private household, so she is a kind of teacher.

clue.text: Clown's depressed

indicators.note: read as 'has': the first word has the second inside it

parts.note: the letters sit inside this word, between its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A sad clown, the classic figure hiding melancholy behind the greasepaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'Clown has depressed': the answer is inside the clown.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling low is an everyday way of saying feeling down or dispirited, so it matches depressed as an adjective.

clue.text: Looking up debtor — a student — not quite lame duck

indicators.note: falling just short of complete, so the final letter is dropped
in a down clue, looking up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: DR is the accounting abbreviation for debtor
taken as written
L is a learner, as on British learner-driver plates
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A lame duck, a student in debt, is looking things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lame duck' reads as a phrase for a failure, but lame is wordplay and duck alone is the definition; the whole string is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The mallard is the commonest wild duck, the green-headed bird of parks and ponds, so it is an example.

clue.text: Surrender legal case about British money

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: a suit is a lawsuit, a case in court
B is the abbreviation for British
M is the abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Someone gives up a lawsuit over British money.
explanation.walkthrough: The lawsuit wraps round B and M.
explanation.definitionFit: To submit is to yield to authority or force, the same verb sense as to surrender.

clue.text: Superhero's attendant

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the caped crusader of the comics
second meaning: an officer's personal servant in the British army

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as Robin, the superhero's sidekick; in fact the 's is 'is', joining two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The comic-book hero shares his name with the soldier assigned to look after an army officer's kit and needs.

clue.text: Order eggs flipped, showing affirmation

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: law and order go together; law is order imposed
ova is Latin for eggs

explanation.surface: Someone orders eggs flipped over easy at a diner, confirming it firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: Order and eggs look like a breakfast request, and flipped like a cooking instruction; all three are wordplay, and the whole joined string is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: An avowal is an open declaration or statement that something is true, which is what an affirmation is.

clue.text: A fling with almost entirely inflexible, unscrupulous lawyer

indicators.note: almost the whole thing but not quite, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: a shy is a throw, as at a coconut shy
stern means rigid or inflexible; its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A brief affair with a rigid, crooked lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: A fling looks like a love affair, but it is a throw; a coconut shy is a British fairground stall where you throw balls at coconuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A shyster is slang for a lawyer who uses shady, dishonest methods, exactly an unscrupulous one.

clue.text: Reprobate son taking daughter's place during meal

indicators.note: taking someone's place means standing in for them, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
an evening meal; its D, short for daughter, is the letter swapped out

explanation.surface: A wayward son takes his sister's seat at the dinner table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' reads like a timing word in the family scene; it only says the swap happens in the meal word.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled person, and a sinner, one who does wrong, is a near synonym.

clue.text: Ace trio modelled for saucy material

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the letters are formed into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: Three top models posed for a racy magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Modelled suggests posing for photographs, fitting the saucy scene, but it is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Erotica is writing or pictures meant to arouse sexual desire, which a cheeky phrase like saucy material describes.

clue.text: Embellish stay on part of ship

parts.note: to be somewhere is to stay or remain there
the deck is a floor of a ship

explanation.surface: Decorating the stays, the ropes supporting a ship's mast.
explanation.walkthrough: A stay is also a rope bracing a mast, which fits the ship; here it is a verb meaning remain.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedeck is to adorn or decorate lavishly, as in bedecked with flags, so it matches embellish.

clue.text: Frivolous four interrupt rehearsal

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a trial run is a rehearsal
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A silly foursome keep disrupting the rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: Four looks like a group of people interrupting; it is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial things are of little importance or seriousness, which is the sense of frivolous as an adjective.

clue.text: Struggle to hold cross new reindeer

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it inside, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: to vie is to compete or struggle
an X is a cross
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A struggle to restrain an angry new reindeer.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross looks like the adjective angry, but it is the letter shaped like a cross. Vixen is one of Santa's reindeer in the poem 'A Visit from St Nicholas'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vixen is named among Santa's team of reindeer alongside Dasher and Dancer, so it is an example of a reindeer.

clue.text: Perfume coming from market trader's stand thanks to me

indicators.note: one thing going to another means it is changed into it

parts.note: a stall is where a market trader sells
ta is British slang for thanks
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopper enjoys the scent of a market perfume stall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thanks to me' reads as the setter taking credit; it is the instruction to change the letters for thanks into the word me.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfume can mean a sweet scent in the air, and a smell is any odour, so the nouns match.

clue.text: In London 007 spelled out a mode of dispatch

indicators.note: the answer lies in the run of letters that follows, so only a stretch of them is kept

parts.note: only the final letter falls inside the run
the number written as it is said, oh oh seven; the run stops partway through seven

explanation.surface: James Bond, 007, explains a method of killing in London.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a hidden word in disguise: write 007 out as it is said, oh oh seven, and the answer runs through LondoN OO SEven. Dispatch means kill here, not post.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispatch is a euphemism for killing, and hanging with a rope loop was a method of execution.

clue.text: See 20
Reduce European investment in party before team become old-fashioned

indicators.note: investing puts something inside a venture, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: a do is a party
a cricket or football team has eleven players, XI in Roman numerals
clothes date when they go out of fashion
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Cutting European money put into a party that is going stale.
explanation.walkthrough: Reduce looks like cut spending; in chemistry reduction means removing oxygen, and that is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry, to reduce a compound is to strip oxygen from it, which is what this technical verb names.

clue.text: Question about rucksack's content

indicators.note: the content of something is what lies inside it
turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the letters sit inside, read from right to left

explanation.surface: Someone queries what is in a rucksack.
explanation.walkthrough: Question looks like a noun but is the verb; read rucKSAck backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To question someone is to put inquiries to them, the same verb sense as to ask.

clue.text: Cream tea, extremely deficient and low in calories

indicators.note: lacking at the extremes, so both end letters are missing

parts.note: the word with both its ends gone
lite is the marketing spelling for reduced-calorie food

explanation.surface: A cream tea that is short on calories, a dieter's dream.
explanation.walkthrough: A cream tea is a British afternoon tea of scones, jam and clotted cream; here Cream stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of a group is its best part, and the elite are the select best, so both mean the top few.

clue.text: By which I mean an offence

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, the same as a
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: A speaker clarifies that they meant to call something an offence.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a clarification, and the first four words are one definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to clarify, as in 'bank, as in river bank', which is exactly saying what one means.

clue.text: Creep dropping behind student brainbox?

indicators.note: dropping the behind means losing the rear, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to skulk is to creep about furtively; its last letter goes
L is a learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: A creep falling behind a clever student, a swot.
explanation.walkthrough: Brainbox is slang for a clever person, but read literally it is the box holding the brain; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The cranium is the bony case that holds the brain, so it is quite literally a box for brains.

clue.text: Unlit, deserted animal sanctuary

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for deserted
Noah's ark was the refuge for the animals

explanation.surface: An abandoned animal refuge standing in darkness.
explanation.walkthrough: The animal sanctuary is not a modern rescue centre but Noah's vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhere unlit has no lights on, which is the everyday adjective meaning without light.
